value.question: Compare BM25 keyword search with dense embedding retrieval, and say in which situations each is the better choice.

steps.description: Search for general technical comparisons of BM25 keyword search vs dense embedding/vector retrieval, focusing on how each works, their strengths and weaknesses
Fetch relevant technical pages (blog posts, academic papers, documentation) comparing BM25 and dense retrieval, including benchmarks and use-case guidance
Search for current best practices and hybrid retrieval approaches that combine BM25 with dense embeddings, to inform when each is the better choice

key_findings: BM25 excels at low-latency lexical matching and precise term-level recall on static corpora, delivering predictable latency and simpler governance, while dense retrieval using semantic embeddings unlocks cross-document semantic matching and robust recall when vocabulary or context evolve, but with higher compute costs and more complex freshness requirements (fetch-54781a1a03da).

Dense-only retrieval fails on rare identifiers — product codes, error numbers, regulatory clause references, or names — because embeddings encode meaning not exact strings; the exact-match document with the literal string gets out-ranked by semantically similar but incorrect passages, while the reverse failure occurs when a user query shares no token overlap with the relevant article, so BM25 returns nothing useful (fetch-a4f39f5641c1).

A concrete failure example is 'HTTP 503' vs 'HTTP/2' having high semantic similarity (both contain 'HTTP'), so vector embeddings miss the specific error term, whereas BM25's exact term matching with intelligent weighting penalizes common terms and rewards unique ones, which matters for technical documentation with specific error codes, version numbers, and API names (fetch-52348cb90f18).

In practice the recommended approach is a hybrid pipeline that starts with BM25 for baseline speed, layers in dense retrieval where semantic gaps hinder relevance, and fuses the two via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), with benchmark evidence showing a tuned hybrid reaching 0.7497 NDCG — a 7.4% lift over either BM25 (0.6983) or pure vector search (0.6953) alone (fetch-54781a1a03da, fetch-52348cb90f18, fetch-a4f39f5641c1).
gaps: The evidence does not provide specific operational guidance on how to tune the hybrid fusion (e.g., RRF weights) or how to monitor for drift and data freshness in a live pipeline, though production guidance is promised.
No cost or latency benchmarks are given for either method in production-scale systems beyond qualitative statements that BM25 has modest compute and dense retrieval has higher compute costs.

The evidence is largely from practitioner blogs and vendor comparisons; no independent, peer-reviewed or vendor-neutral benchmark validation is provided beyond the single WANDS e-commerce NDCG figure cited from a third-party source.

The material does not address how the choice between BM25 and dense retrieval interacts with different data types (e.g., images, structured records, multilingual content) or with varying corpus sizes and update velocities.

value.text: BM25 keyword search is the better choice for low-latency, precise term-level matching on technical or code-heavy content — error codes, version numbers, API names, product identifiers — where exact strings matter and vocabulary is static or slowly evolving. Dense embedding retrieval is the better choice when users express intent in conversational language that shares no token overlap with the relevant document, and where semantics and cross-document recall are needed. Each has a distinct failure mode: dense-only search misses rare literal identifiers, while BM25 returns nothing when no words overlap. Because neither wins across all query types, the recommended production approach is hybrid retrieval, starting with BM25 for baseline speed and layering in dense retrieval where semantic gaps hurt relevance, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Note that situational guidance beyond these categories remains unverified by the fetched evidence.

key_points: BM25 gives exact term matching with intelligent weighting, penalizing common terms and rewarding unique ones — suited to technical docs with error codes, version numbers, and API names.
Dense retrieval captures semantic equivalence and finds relevant passages even with zero token overlap, at higher compute cost and with freshness requirements.
Dense-only retrieval fails on rare identifiers (product codes, error numbers, names) because embeddings encode meaning, not exact strings.
The practical recommendation is hybrid retrieval: BM25 baseline plus dense retrieval, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
